column1: # The cross-connection trial on the animal branch (docs/UPPER.md §17, question 52, option B).
# One row per candidate edge sub ⊑ sup, where sup is a class of align/trial-cross-classes.tsv
# or one of core's own classes `pet` and `livestock`.
# wikidata  y: Wikidata's subclass statements (P279, transitively) lead from the concept's item
#              to the class's item, as fetched on 2026-11-12 after the items of fourteen animals
#              were corrected (align/overrides.tsv: `eagle` had a gold coin's, `lamb` the
# tree      y: WordNet 3.1's own tree leads from the concept's synset to a synset that says what
#              the class says: aquatic vertebrate, aquatic mammal or aquatic bird for
#              aquatic-animal, ratite for flightless-bird, carnivore (its flesh-eating order of
#              mammals), ruminant, bird of prey, domestic animal; -: it does not. Every edge the
#              tree states from a kind to a class is a row, unless a kind above it has the edge.
#              WordNet's `shellfish` is another word for mollusk, which takes in the octopus and
#              the garden snail; it is not the class here and is not counted.
# gloss     y: the WordNet gloss of the sense the node has states the quality outright; hedged:
#              it states it with "mostly", "usually", "some", "or"; -: it does not state it. The
#              whole gloss is read. align/concepts.tsv keeps its first 97 characters, and for
#              `pig` and `guinea-pig` it keeps the gloss of the person their rows once meant.
# The three readings are Claude's (2026-11-12), each of the edge with every ancestor it brings in:
# strict    y: true of every kind the word covers, with no exception known; n: a kind is known,
#              or held on good grounds, to fall outside the class. The word is read in its
#              everyday sense and the kind in its grown, natural state: a chick that cannot yet
#              fly and a caged tiger that is fed are no exceptions. This is the standard a pack
#              is held to (Peter, 2026-11-12): an edge with a counterexample stays out, and
#              whoever wants it adds it to a store of their own.
#              A kind that lets its body cool while it rests and warms it again by its own
#              heat (a bat, a mouse in torpor) is warm-blooded all the same. In doubt the
# everyday  y: true of the word in its everyday sense, the standard v14 was read by
#              (under which goose ⊑ poultry stands, though wild geese are no poultry).
# typical   y: what people say of the kind; n marks a claim that is simply wrong.
# A candidate is here because a source proposes it or because the reading finds it typical.
# The mammal kinds under `warm-blooded-animal` came on 2026-11-13, when Peter decided question
# 53 (no exceptions): the line that fails of `mammal` is said of each kind it is true of.
# The edges that hold in the everyday reading with no source behind them have Peter's
